説明: This blog's term for Japan's unwritten cultural framework, rooted in Shintō values of harmony, purity, and relational balance.
(1930–2017) Japanese-born American anthropologist who theorized 'social relativism' in Japanese Patterns of Behavior (1976).
(1976) Lebra's anthropological study of Japanese interpersonal conduct, built on the concept of 'social relativism' (behavior shaped by social context).
Japanese anthropologist who proposed 'reference-other orientation' in Japanese Sense of Self (1992), describing selfhood defined through others' perspectives.
Shintō sun goddess, mythic ancestor of the imperial line, enshrined at Ise Jingū and recorded in the Kojiki.
Shintō storm god and Amaterasu's brother, whose violent misconduct drives her into a cave in the Kojiki myth.
Buddhist doctrine that good and bad deeds bring matching consequences; in everyday Japanese, often means 'you reap what you sow.'
Shintō notion of ritual impurity or depleted spiritual energy, linked to death, illness, and misfortune, and removed through purification rites.
Japan's indigenous religious tradition, centered on kami (deities and sacred presences), shrine worship, seasonal festivals, and purification rites.
Shintō purification rite, performed by a priest, that removes sin and impurity (tsumi and kegare) before festivals and worship.
Everyday or ritual cleansing in Shintō practice, such as scattering salt or rinsing with water, to remove impurity.
Shintō purification by immersing the body in a river, waterfall, or sea; figuratively, atonement after wrongdoing, especially by public figures.
Shintō idea that kami dwell in mountains, trees, tools, and ancestors; 'yaoyorozu' means an uncountable multitude, not a literal number.
Belief that natural phenomena, places, and objects possess spirits or souls; term popularized by anthropologist E. B. Tylor (1871).
Spirits said to awaken in tools and household objects after about a hundred years of use; a Muromachi-era folklore theme.
Religion founded by Siddhārtha Gautama in ancient India; it reached Japan in the 6th century and blended with Shintō.
Chinese ethical and social philosophy of Confucius, stressing roles, duty, and hierarchy; it shaped Edo-period education and samurai ethics.
Chinese tradition centered on the Tao (the Way) and naturalness; it influenced Japanese calendars, divination, and seasonal customs.
Japanese system of divination and cosmology based on yin-yang and the Five Phases, used at court for calendars and fortune-telling.
Medieval doctrine that Shintō kami are local manifestations (suijaku) of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, who are their 'original ground' (honji).
Syncretic blending of Shintō and Buddhism, common from the Nara period; officially ended by the Meiji separation orders of 1868.
Ideal of everlasting freshness maintained through periodic renewal, closely associated with the rebuilding of Ise Jingū every twenty years.
Shintō's most sacred shrine complex, in Mie Prefecture; the inner shrine honors Amaterasu, and buildings are rebuilt every twenty years.
Ritual rebuilding of Ise Jingū's buildings and transfer of the deity every twenty years, continued since the late 7th century.

読み: ポケットモンスター / ポケモン
説明: Media franchise launched in 1996 with Game Boy games by Game Freak; the name contracts 'Pocket Monsters' (Poketto Monsutā).
Fire-type canine Pokémon, introduced in Generation I and resembling a guardian lion; its Pokédex species is 'Legendary Pokémon.'
Electric-type Legendary Pokémon, a tiger-like beast of thunder; one of the three Legendary Beasts introduced in Generation II.
Fire-type Legendary Pokémon, a lion-like beast of volcanoes; one of the three Legendary Beasts of Generation II.
Water-type Legendary Pokémon, a canine beast said to purify water; one of the three Legendary Beasts of Generation II.
Electric/Ghost-type Pokémon, a plasma being that possesses appliances such as ovens and washing machines and changes form accordingly.
Ghost/Steel-type Pokémon, a sword inhabited by a spirit; it evolves into Doublade and then Aegislash.
Ghost/Fire-type Pokémon resembling a chandelier, whose flames are said to absorb the spirits of the dead; introduced in Generation V.
Recurring in-game facility where players restore their Pokémon's health for free; also the name of Japan's official Pokémon retail stores.
(1965–) Japanese game designer, founder of Game Freak, and creator of Pokémon, inspired by his childhood insect collecting.
Buddhist concept that all conditioned things are impermanent; a classic literary theme, as in The Tale of the Heike.
Literally 'self-restraint police': coined during the COVID-19 pandemic for citizens who pressure or shame others into observing voluntary restrictions.

読み: パーシヴァル・ローウェル
説明: (1855–1916) American businessman and astronomer who founded Lowell Observatory; he wrote about Japan after living there in the 1880s.

用語: The Soul of the Far East
説明: (1888) Lowell's book on Japan and East Asia, arguing that Far Eastern societies suppress individuality in favor of impersonality.

読み: ルース・ベネディクト
説明: (1887–1948) American cultural anthropologist whose wartime study of Japan classified it as a 'shame culture,' contrasted with Western 'guilt cultures.'
'Shame culture': Benedict's classification of societies where conduct is governed by fear of public disgrace rather than internalized guilt.
(1946) Benedict's study of Japanese culture, commissioned by the U.S. Office of War Information and written without fieldwork in Japan.
(1862–1933) Japanese educator and diplomat, a League of Nations Under-Secretary-General, who wrote Bushido in English for Western readers.
(1900) Nitobe's English-language book presenting bushidō, the samurai moral code, to Western readers as the ethical foundation of Japan.
(1862–1913) Japanese art critic and philosopher who helped found the Tokyo School of Fine Arts and promoted Asian aesthetics abroad.
(1906) Okakura's English-language essay presenting the tea ceremony as a philosophy of simplicity, imperfection, and Asian aesthetics.
(1659–1719) Samurai of the Saga domain who became a Buddhist monk after his lord's death; his talks became Hagakure.

用語: Hagakure: The Book of the Samurai
説明: (1716) Reflections of Yamamoto Tsunetomo on samurai conduct, recorded by Tashiro Tsuramoto; it stresses loyalty and readiness for death.
(1925–1970) Japanese novelist and playwright, author of The Temple of the Golden Pavilion, known for traditionalist aesthetics and nationalism.
Literally 'air': a group's unspoken mood that individuals feel pressured to sense and follow; 'reading the air' means perceiving it.
Japanese concept of the meaningful interval between things, in space or time; deliberately shaped in architecture, calligraphy, theater, and conversation.
(1884–1955) German philosopher who studied archery in Japan under Awa Kenzō and wrote Zen in the Art of Archery.
(1880–1939) Japanese kyūdō master who taught shooting as a spiritual practice; teacher of Eugen Herrigel in Sendai.
Zen term meaning 'nothing' or 'not,' famously used in the kōan of Jōshū's dog, pointing beyond being versus non-being.
(574–622) Prince-regent of Asuka-period Japan, traditionally credited with the Seventeen-Article Constitution, which opens by prizing harmony (wa).
Japanese martial ways such as kendō, jūdō, and kyūdō, pursued as lifelong disciplines of character and self-cultivation, beyond combat skill.
Japanese arts such as tea ceremony, calligraphy, and Nō theater, practiced as lifelong paths of discipline and self-cultivation.
'Way' or 'path': a practice pursued as lifelong discipline, as in chadō, shodō, and budō; the Japanese reading of Tao.
Imperial capital of Japan from 794 to 1868, known for temples, shrines, and traditional crafts; site of UNESCO-listed historic monuments.
'Optimization': adjusting a system for maximum efficiency, a modern managerial and technological ideal; the essays contrast it with sustained practice.
Literally 'tuning': adjusting an instrument such as a piano to pitch; used here for calmly aligning oneself with present reality.
Ordinary profit: operating profit adjusted for recurring non-operating items such as interest, a standard Japanese measure of steady earning power.
Depreciation: the accounting practice of spreading an asset's cost over its useful life, so recorded value declines yearly.
Japanese repair of broken ceramics with lacquer dusted in gold, leaving the cracks visible as part of the object's history.
French adjective for a surface softened by age and use, valued as proof of lived character; used of leather, wood.
Hermès's creative line, launched in 2010, that transforms surplus materials such as leather, silk, and crystal into unique objects.
Japanese for 'technique' or 'art': a learned method for achieving a practical end, as in jūjutsu; contrasts with dō.
(1994–) Japanese two-way baseball star (pitcher and hitter) in Major League Baseball, noted for his disciplined, process-focused approach.
(1934–2021) Hungarian-American psychologist who developed the concept of 'flow,' a state of complete absorption in an activity.
Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, responsible for health care, labor policy, social security, and national demographic statistics.

読み: 高度経済成長期 [Kōdo Keizai Seichōki]
説明: Japan's era of rapid economic growth, roughly 1955 to 1973, which shaped lifetime employment and the postwar corporate system.
(1868) Political change that ended the Tokugawa shogunate and restored imperial rule, launching rapid modernization and Westernization.
(1985–) Tokyo animation studio founded by Miyazaki Hayao, Takahata Isao, and Suzuki Toshio; known for hand-drawn feature films.

読み: 『千と千尋の神隠し』 [Sen to Chihiro no Kamikakushi]
説明: (2001) Miyazaki's Academy Award–winning animated film in which a girl works in a bathhouse for spirits to rescue her parents.
Ten-year-old protagonist of Spirited Away who enters the spirit world, takes the name Sen, and rescues her parents.
Japanese public bathhouse; in Spirited Away, the spirits' bathhouse run by Yubāba, where Chihiro works.
Sorceress who runs the bathhouse in Spirited Away and controls her workers by taking their names.
The name Yubāba leaves Chihiro after taking the rest of her name; the character 千 means 'thousand.'
(1941–) Japanese animator and director, co-founder of Studio Ghibli; films include My Neighbor Totoro and Spirited Away.
